Subfactors, index and finite-depth classification

Paths, local projections and a faithful trace

The index restriction came from positivity. To construct examples, we need positive models of the same relations. A path graph supplies both the Hilbert spaces and the coefficients of the projections. Its positive eigenvector supplies the trace.

We assume Matrix inclusions and the Markov trace, the Perron–Frobenius theorem cited there, and the tracial GNS construction. The general definition of an AF algebra and the description of its traces by compatible finite-level traces are in Sections 4 and 10 of AF algebras. We use those interfaces and prove the local projection and trace assertions needed here. Basic references are [Jones] and [Wenzl].

Construction and proof sources: Propositions 9.1–9.2 and Theorem 9.3 below construct the positive graph weights, path matrix units and local projections. Theorems 9.4–9.6 prove endpoint generation, the faithful Markov trace and the finite-graph trace conclusion, with the scalar endpoint stated separately. Proposition 9.7 and the later coordinate formulas retain the full boundary and path-length conventions. The finite inclusion and trace interfaces come from Matrix inclusions and the Markov trace; the infinite-path factoriality is proved in The trace and the tail of a path. Jones and Wenzl retain their projection-model credit. Takesaki, Chapter XIX, Theorem 3.1 and §3, printed pages 441–465 is the comparison for the path and projection conventions, including the explicit corrections below.

Its norm is one by (9.1). This proves selfadjointness and idempotence. Operators at distance at least two change different middle vertices, preserve each other's endpoint tests, and have unchanged coefficients; hence they commute.

Theorem 9.4. These projections generate every finite path algebra:

Proof. The assertion starts with . Suppose it holds for . If is reachable in steps, choose such a path . For any two length- paths ending at , let their penultimate vertices be , and their length- prefixes be . The embedded matrix units

belong to . The coefficient is positive. The backtrack test in excludes every other final vertex, so this identity holds in the full algebra, not merely in its -block.

Thus contains every matrix block whose endpoint was reachable two levels earlier. In a rooted line graph, there is at most one remaining endpoint: the new vertex , if present. Only the path reaches it, so its block is scalar. The identity minus the identities of the already obtained blocks supplies this scalar block. If the finite graph has no new endpoint, all blocks have already been obtained. Hence , completing the induction.

The rooted-line hypothesis matters here. A graph with branching can have several new blocks, which a single identity cannot separate.

The finite graph has just one trace

Theorem 9.6. The AF algebra for has a unique tracial state. It is the trace (9.6). For , its tracial von Neumann algebra is an approximately finite-dimensional II₁ factor. For , the path algebra and its von Neumann closure are .

Proof. After level , every vertex of the appropriate parity is reachable. The inclusion matrices then alternate between a fixed bipartite adjacency matrix and . On one parity the two-step restriction matrix is , or . The explicit parity spectra in Proposition 9.7 below show that has a simple largest eigenvalue , a strictly positive eigenvector given by the corresponding entries of , and all other eigenvalues strictly smaller. Thus, for that vector ,

This also covers the zero eigenvalue on the larger parity when the graph has an odd number of vertices.

Let be the minimal-projection trace vector of any tracial state at a stabilized level. Compatibility gives for every , with and nonzero. The normalized image of the nonnegative cone under converges uniformly to the Perron ray. Indeed, write its image as a nonnegative combination of the columns of ; after normalization it is a convex combination of the normalized columns, and each column converges to the same strictly positive Perron vector. Therefore lies on that ray. Its normalization fixes the scalar. Earlier levels follow by restriction, proving uniqueness.

Let . Its normal trace is faithful. A nontrivial central projection would give a different tracial state on . Uniqueness forces on , hence on by normality. Taking gives , a contradiction. Thus is a factor.

For , . Equation (9.7), with finitely many bounded vertex weights, implies that the block sizes are unbounded. Faithfulness embeds these matrix blocks in , so cannot be a finite-dimensional factor. A finite infinite-dimensional factor is II₁. The increasing union of the finite-dimensional is weakly dense, which is the asserted approximation property.

For , the graph has only and . Exactly one path exists at every length, , and every . Thus every .

This endpoint corrects the II₁ assertion in Takesaki's Theorem XIX.3.1 when its parameter is : the stated projection-generated model has index parameter one and is scalar. The index-one II₁ example is instead the identity inclusion . No nontrivial construction is needed for that inclusion.

For the infinite graph there are many tracial states on the AF algebra. The Markov trace (9.6) is factorial, but uniqueness of all tracial states is not the reason. We prove factoriality in The trace and the tail of a path.

Transposition exposes the endpoint condition. If denotes the last coordinate vector in , then

Indeed, all interior coordinates use two neighboring sine values; the final coordinate lacks the displayed sine term. At , the first missing term vanishes. Combining that transposed identity with (9.13) gives the two eigenvector equations and (9.14). For , these angles lie strictly between zero and , so the eigenvalues are positive and distinct in decreasing order. Both vectors are nonzero. Distinct eigenvalues give independent eigenvectors, exhausting each -dimensional space.

At , the second missing term vanishes, giving the asserted eigenvector equations. The positive eigenvalues are again distinct. At the remaining frequency , and , which annihilates. This supplies the last eigenvector of ; the dimension count proves completeness.

At frequency , every retained sine coordinate is strictly positive. Each matrix is real symmetric, so eigenvectors for any other eigenvalue are orthogonal to this vector. A nonzero nonnegative vector cannot be orthogonal to a strictly positive vector. Simplicity of the top eigenvalue therefore proves the last assertion.

The positivity assertion concerns eigenvectors of the full square matrices. A truncated sine vector can be positive at several frequencies. For example, take and . Thus the statement “only ” in the rectangular parts of Takesaki's Lemma XIX.3.8 needs the full endpoint eigenvector condition; the displayed one-direction identities themselves are valid.

Exercise 9.3 — intermediate. Why does the scalar frontier block in Theorem 9.4 disappear after the finite graph is fully reached?
